title: The Social Sector of the Economy: The Missing Piece Facing the Market
author: Óscar David Rojas Silva
content:
_This article by Óscar David Rojas Silva originally appeared in the[July 23,
2026 edition of Contralínea](https://contralinea.com.mx/opinion/articulo/el-
sector-social-de-la-economia-la-pieza-que-falta-frente-al-mercado/), an
independent Mexican investigative journalism magazine._

Starting in the 1980s, neoliberalism took hold in universities, according to
the work of Sarah Babb [1]. The measurement method used was to analyze the
main theorist cited in the theses produced by the Faculty of Economics at
UNAM. What this author found was an undeniable break. Whereas from the 1940s
to the 1970s the dominant authors were Marx and Keynes, by the lost decade the
visions coming from the Austrian School or the University of Chicago began to
dominate, as in the case of Milton Friedman or Hayek. This shift also led to a
migration from the analysis of political economy, history, philosophy,
anthropology, etc. to the inhospitable and cold territories of the econometric
model. The science, which previously had at its center the concrete discussion
of the State and social problems, was reduced to an abstract discussion of the
productivity and rationality that individuals and firms should adopt in order
to reach the mythical state of equilibrium.

It was not only Marx, but also Keynes, who were exiled from the epistemic and
pedagogical core of the public university. As a consequence, the social sector
of the economy was completely erased; every social problem became a stochastic
variable within the framework of sterile artifacts of hypermathematization.
This, of course, was not accidental, nor simply a course taken by the personal
vision of its administrators; it was in fact a great campaign of
homogenization under the new paradigm of the market. The damage became the
rule in practically the majority of economics schools around the world. The
Nobel Prize system plus the oligopolistic control of publishers, journals, and
leadership positions made it possible to fully establish that model. The
social sector was forgotten and marginalized.

To define the concept, the social sector represents all those forms that do
not compulsively pursue the objectives of the capitalist economy. They have as
their antecedent all the community and cooperative forms that have not been
able to be subsumed under the logic of profit. But we must add that the
phenomenon of those forms that are in open conflict under a process of
exploitation also enters here, that is, the field of daily work in private
companies in which the struggle is for a decent wage. It might seem to be a
matter of the private sector, but no, it is also a matter of the social
sector.

To expand on this discussion, we must distinguish between the meaning of the
corporate private at the scale of large transnational companies, and what
small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) mean for the economic metabolism of
the different communities. The former is entirely corporate, that is,
specialized in immediate speculative profits; the latter correspond to
multiple social objectives, which is why this sphere coincides better with the
sphere of the social sector. The objective of the collective worker is the
reproduction of life, not of capital.

If we consider our conceptualization of a mixed social economy, we observe the
three components of the organic economic totality: the state sector, the
private sector, and the social sector. The installed neoclassical economics
applied a collective epistemicide; it made the issues of the State disappear
and attacked them while minimizing the civilizational consequences of the
market economy on the population. The dream of progress and the arrival at the
supposed modernity of the developed first world was installed in the common
imaginary; the economy was then limited to the study of the exclusive needs of
the private sector. Hence economic science is confused with a matter of
business.

In the face of this crisis, reality itself has taken it upon itself to
contradict the automatism and reductionism of this vision. As of today, the
renewed centrality of the State in the economy is beyond discussion, as is a
widespread concern for the consequences of that development in the realm of
ecology, of political relations, and of interpersonal relations. There is talk
not only of identity rights but also of essential economic rights that
populations demand: education, health, housing, pensions, etc.; an
accumulation of needs with chronic problems, always contrasting with the
accelerated concentration of wealth in a compact core of the 1 percent.

That is, reality has already generated a structural change on the side of
concerns, but it is still necessary that the methods of study also mutate.
Today the voices of the Nobel laureates no longer mean much to the community,
but there still remains a bureaucracy that, due to the verticality of its
structures, hardly finds the internal incentives to renew itself radically.
For this reason it is necessary to promote changes in the study programs, not
only with the consideration of the topics, but also with the guarantee of
epistemological plurality that allows national problems to be addressed from
an adequate perspective, that is, not through the vision of the private
sector, nor exclusively through the structural approach of the public sector,
but through the social sector itself.

There are three elements that I highlight to broaden the perspective of the
mixed functioning of the economy. The first is the reform of Article 2 of the
Constitution, which recognized Indigenous and Afro-Mexican peoples and
communities as subjects of public law, which gave rise to the Fund of
Contributions for Social Infrastructure for Indigenous and Afro-Mexican
Peoples (FAISPIAM), with a budget for 2026 of 13.5 billion pesos that the
communities themselves will decide on in assembly [2]. On the other hand,
there is the 2024 reform of Articles 4 and 27, which elevated the Programs for
Well-Being to the rank of a constitutional right—universal pension for older
adults, pension for people with disabilities, Sembrando Vida, fertilizers, and
guaranteed prices—and shielded their budget, which today amounts to
practically 1 trillion pesos, an amount that can no longer be reduced in real
terms from one year to the next. And, in third place, we have a systematic
recovery of the minimum wage, reduction of the workday, profit-sharing,
pension reforms, and promotion of union democratization that strengthen the
labor world in our country.

In these cases the same underlying movement occurs: what neoclassical
economics treated as discretionary welfare spending becomes a constituted
right, exactly the displacement that this paradigm had made unthinkable. In
fact, the relevance of this mixed recovery is to recall the basic meaning of
the social sciences: to know concrete reality in order to be able to transform
it; there is no sense, for example, in the growth of GDP if it is not
reflected in the sustained improvement of the living conditions of the people.
A compelling piece of data on this trend is the 13.4 million Mexicans who left
multidimensional poverty since 2018. Recovering this vision now broadens our
horizon to identify the new processes and the new ways of measuring them over
time; it is about the need not only to distinguish between growth and
development, but to give social content to the latter.

All this new need is already occurring in the face of the intense global
crisis we are experiencing, which is why the change of methods in the
universities must hasten its pace in order to also fulfill its objective as
part of this third sector: to incorporate cooperativism, the social economy,
and critical thinking into the curriculum, and thus generate the conditions
for the community to achieve ever deeper transformations.

_Óscar David Rojas Silva is an economist (UdeG) with a master 's and doctorate
(UNAM) in the critique of political economy. He is an academic at FES Acatlán,
Director of the Center for the Study of Contemporary Capitalism, and a
communicator specialized in critical thinking at Radio del Azufre and Academia
del Azufre._
